hmmt-feb-2012-geo-01.title: Area ratio
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-01.body:
$[ABC]=\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2$ and $[AEDB]+[EDC]=[ABC]$, with $[AEDB]=2[EDC]$, so $[EDC]=\frac23$.

Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $E$ to $BC$. Since $\angle C=45^\circ$, $EF=FC$. Also $DC=1$, so $[EDC]=\frac12\cdot EF\cdot DC=\frac{EF}2=\frac23$, giving $EF=FC=\frac43$. Then $FD=FC-DC=\frac13$ and
$$DE=\sqrt{EF^2+FD^2}=\sqrt{\frac{16}9+\frac19}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}3.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}3$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-01.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-01.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $A=(0,2)$, $C=(2,0)$, $D=(1,0)$, and $E=(t,2-t)$ on $AC$. Then $[ECD]=\frac12\cdot DC\cdot(2-t)=\frac{2-t}2$. As in the first solution $[ECD]=\frac23$, so $t=\frac23$ and $E=\left(\frac23,\frac43\right)$. Hence
$$DE^2=\left(\tfrac13\right)^2+\left(\tfrac43\right)^2=\frac{17}9,\qquad DE=\frac{\sqrt{17}}3.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}3$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-02.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-02.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,2)$. $BC$ has direction $(-1,2)$, so $\ell$ has direction $(2,1)$: $\ell=\{(2s,s)\}$. The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is $x=\frac12$, meeting $\ell$ at $E=(\frac12,\frac14)$; that of $AC$ is $y=1$, meeting $\ell$ at $F=(2,1)$. Then
$$EF=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac32\right)^2+\left(\tfrac34\right)^2}=\frac34\sqrt5.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt5}4$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-02.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-02.body:
Let $M,N$ be the midpoints of $AB,AC$. Since $\ell\perp BC$, $\angle EAB=\angle ACB$, and triangle $AEM$ is similar to $CBA$, so $AE=AM\cdot\frac{CB}{CA}=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt5}2=\frac{\sqrt5}4$. Similarly $\angle FAC=\angle ABC$ and $FAN\sim CBA$ gives $AF=AN\cdot\frac{BC}{BA}=\sqrt5$. $E$ and $F$ are on the same ray from $A$, so $EF=AF-AE=\frac{3\sqrt5}4$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt5}4$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-03.title: Angle chase
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-03.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle BAC$. Because $D$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AI$, $DA=DI$, so $\angle DIA=\angle DAI=\frac\alpha2$ and the exterior angle gives $\angle IDB=\alpha$. Since $BD=BI$, $\angle BID=\angle BDI=\alpha$, hence $\angle DBI=180^\circ-2\alpha$ and $\angle ABC=2\angle DBI=360^\circ-4\alpha$.

In the same way $\angle ACB=360^\circ-4\alpha$. The angle sum gives $\alpha+2(360^\circ-4\alpha)=180^\circ$, i.e. $720^\circ-7\alpha=180^\circ$ and
$$\alpha=\frac{540}7^\circ.$$
(Then $\angle B=\angle C=\frac{360}7^\circ$, an isosceles triangle with $D,E$ inside the sides, so this value is attained.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{540}7$ degrees**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-04.title: Power of a point and similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-04.body:
$AB$ is tangent to $\omega_2$ at $A$, so by power of the point $B$: $BA^2=BD\cdot BC=3\cdot16=48$, $BA=4\sqrt3$.

Because $BC$ is tangent to $\omega_1$ at $B$, the tangent-chord angle gives $\angle DBE=\angle BAE=\angle BAD$. Triangles $DBE$ and $DAB$ share the angle at $D$, so $\triangle DEB\sim\triangle DBA$, and
$$\frac{EB}{ED}=\frac{BA}{BD}=\frac{4\sqrt3}3.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{4\sqrt3}3$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-05.title: The dark disk has half the radius
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-05.body:
Let the cage have radius $R$. The beam is centered $37.5^\circ$ from the diameter through the flashlight and is $15^\circ$ wide, so its rays make angles $\theta\in[30^\circ,45^\circ]$ with that diameter. A ray at angle $\theta$ travels along a chord at distance $R\sin\theta$ from the center, so the distances lie in $[\frac R2,\frac R{\sqrt2}]$.

On a reflective wall the next chord of a ray's path is the previous chord rotated about the center, so every chord of that path is at the same distance $d=R\sin\theta$ from the center. Hence no light ever gets closer than $\frac R2$ to the center: the disk of radius $\frac R2$ is dark.

Conversely, take a ray with irrational $\theta/\pi$-type rotation (all but countably many rays in the beam). Its chords are rotations of each other by a fixed irrational angle, hence dense, so they come arbitrarily close to every point of the annulus $d\le r\le R$. Letting $d$ vary over $[\frac R2,\frac R{\sqrt2}]$ gives a dense lit set in the whole annulus $\frac R2<r\le R$, and the lit region is open, so up to area $0$ the whole annulus is lit.

The lit fraction is $\dfrac{\pi R^2-\pi(R/2)^2}{\pi R^2}=\dfrac34$.

**Answer: $\dfrac34$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-06.title: The path is a staircase
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-06.body:
Consecutive segments are perpendicular, so after $X_0X_1$ the path $X_1X_2X_3\dots$ alternates between directions perpendicular and parallel to $X_0X_1$. Since each point lies in the triangle formed by the previous two and $A$, the path is a monotone staircase converging to $A$.

Let $Y$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $X_0X_1$. The staircase from $X_1$ to $A$ has total length $X_1Y$ in the direction of $X_0X_1$ and $YA$ perpendicular to it, so
$$\sum|X_iX_{i+1}|=X_0X_1+X_1Y+YA=X_0Y+YA.$$
Triangle $X_0YA$ has a right angle at $Y$ and hypotenuse $AX_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$. For legs $p,q$ with $p^2+q^2=AX_0^2$ we have $p+q\le\sqrt2\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$, with equality when $p=q$. So
$$\sum|X_iX_{i+1}|\le\sqrt2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt6}3.$$
Equality needs $\angle YX_0A=45^\circ$, i.e. $\angle AX_1X_0=105^\circ$, which is achievable (then $AX_1=\frac{\sin45^\circ}{\sqrt3\sin105^\circ}<1$, so $X_1$ lies on segment $AB$, and the resulting sequence satisfies all the conditions).

I checked numerically that this configuration is valid and gives the sum $0.8165\ldots=\frac{\sqrt6}3$, while other starting angles give smaller valid sums.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt6}3$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-07.title: Which points of $T$ project to a vertex
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-07.body:
$S$ is a cross-polytope with vertices $\pm e_i$, inside the cube whose boundary is $T$. A vertex $v$ of $S$ is the closest point of $S$ to $p$ exactly when $(p-v)\cdot(w-v)\le0$ for every $w\in S$ (the nearest-point condition for a convex set). It suffices to test $w$ at the other vertices of $S$.

Take $v=e_1$. Testing $w=\pm e_i$ ($i\ne1$) gives $(p-e_1)\cdot(\pm e_i-e_1)=1-p_1\pm p_i\le0$, i.e. $|p_i|\le p_1-1$ for all $i\ne1$. Since $p\in T$, some coordinate has absolute value $2$; it cannot be some $p_i$ with $i\ne1$ (that would need $p_1\ge3$), and $p_1=-2$ is impossible. So $p_1=2$ and the conditions become $|p_i|\le1$ for $i=2,\dots,2012$ (testing $w=-e_1$ then holds automatically, and by linearity in $w$ testing the vertices of $S$ suffices).

So the good points near $v=e_1$ form a $2011$-dimensional cube of side $2$ on the face $p_1=2$ (volume $2^{2011}$). There are $2\cdot2012$ vertices, so the good set has total $2011$-dimensional measure $2\cdot2012\cdot2^{2011}$, while $T$ has $2\cdot2012$ faces each of measure $4^{2011}$. The probability is
$$\frac{2\cdot2012\cdot2^{2011}}{2\cdot2012\cdot4^{2011}}=\frac1{2^{2011}}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac1{2^{2011}}$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-08.title: Pitot, Brianchon, similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-08.body:
Since the hexagon has an inscribed circle, tangent lengths give $AB+CD+EF=BC+DE+FA$, so $9+2+4=6+DE+FA$ and $DE+FA=9$. Let $DE=x$, so $FA=9-x$.

By Brianchon's theorem the diagonals $AD,BE,CF$ meet at a point $P$. Because the hexagon is cyclic, the triangles formed with $P$ are similar:
$$\triangle APB\sim\triangle EPD,\qquad \triangle BPC\sim\triangle FPE,\qquad\triangle CPD\sim\triangle APF.$$
From the second: $\frac{BP}{FP}=\frac{BC}{FE}=\frac64=\frac32$; write $BP=3y$, $FP=2y$. From the first: $\frac{AB}{ED}=\frac{PB}{PD}$, so $PD=\frac{3y\cdot x}{9}=\frac{xy}3$. From the third: $\frac{CD}{AF}=\frac{PD}{PF}$, i.e. $\frac2{9-x}=\frac{xy/3}{2y}=\frac x6$, so $x(9-x)=12$, $x^2-9x+12=0$ and
$$x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{33}}2.$$
Both values lie in $(0,9)$ and are swapped by $DE\leftrightarrow FA$, so $\{DE,FA\}=\left\{\frac{9+\sqrt{33}}2,\frac{9-\sqrt{33}}2\right\}$.

**Answer: $\left\{\frac{9+\sqrt{33}}2,\frac{9-\sqrt{33}}2\right\}$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-09.title: Split into four triangles at $O$
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-09.body:
The quadrilateral is the union of triangles $P_1OP_2$, $P_2OP_3$, $P_3OP_4$, $P_4OP_1$, so we maximize each.

Consider $P_1OP_2$ with $A$ on side $P_1P_2$. If $A\ne P_1,P_2$, say $\angle OAP_1<90^\circ$ (so $\angle OAP_2>90^\circ$), then $\angle OO_1P_1=2\angle OAP_1=\angle OO_2P_2$ (inscribed angle at $A$ on each circle), so $\triangle OO_1P_1\sim\triangle OO_2P_2$. This spiral similarity about $O$ gives $\triangle OO_1O_2\sim\triangle OP_1P_2$, hence $\angle P_1OP_2=\angle O_1OO_2=45^\circ$ is fixed. The area is $\frac12\,OP_1\cdot OP_2\sin45^\circ$, which is largest when $OP_1,OP_2$ are the diameters $2OO_1,2OO_2$, i.e. $P_1,P_2$ diametrically opposite $O$. The same holds for the other three triangles.

For this choice $\angle OAP_1=\angle OAP_2=90^\circ$, so $A$ lies on $P_1P_2$, and similarly $B,C,D$ lie on the other sides, so the choice is admissible. The angles at $O$ are $45^\circ,135^\circ,45^\circ,135^\circ$ with $\sin=\frac{\sqrt2}2$ throughout, and the diameters are $2,4,2\sqrt2,4$. The area is
$$\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2\left(2\cdot4+4\cdot2\sqrt2+2\sqrt2\cdot4+4\cdot2\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}4\left(16+16\sqrt2\right)=4\sqrt2+8.$$

**Answer: $8+4\sqrt2$**

hmmt-feb-2012-geo-10.title: Distance from the origin grows by at most $2$ per step
hmmt-feb-2012-geo-10.body:
Let $P_n$ be the circumcenter of $A_nA_{n+1}A_{n+2}$, so $|P_n|\le1$ and $P_nA_n=P_nA_{n+2}$. By the triangle inequality
$$|A_{n+2}|\le|P_n|+P_nA_{n+2}=|P_n|+P_nA_n\le|P_n|+(|A_n|+|P_n|)\le|A_n|+2.$$
Equality holds iff $A_n$, $O=A_0$, $P_n$, $A_{n+2}$ are collinear (in that order) with $|P_n|=1$.

Since $|A_0|=0$, $|A_{2012}|\le2\cdot1006=2012$, so $K=2012^2$ (once the equality case is shown to be realizable).

**Equality case.** $P_0$ is on the unit circle and on the perpendicular bisector of $A_0A_1$, the line $x=\frac12$, so $P_0=\left(\frac12,\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. By reflection in the $x$-axis take $+$. Then $A_0,P_0,A_2$ are collinear and $|A_2|=2$, so $A_2=(1,\sqrt3)$. In general, the collinearity (in the order $A_n,O,P_n,A_{n+2}$) forces $A_{n+2}$ to lie on the ray from $O$ through $P_n$, opposite to $A_n$, at distance $|A_n|+2$. Continuing, $P_{2n}=(-1)^n\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ and by induction $A_{2n}=(-1)^{n+1}(n,\,n\sqrt3)$. Odd-indexed points can be taken as $A_{2n+1}=(-1)^n(n+1,-n\sqrt3)$ with $P_{2n+1}=(-1)^{n+1}\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, making every condition hold.

For $n=1006$: $A_{2012}=(-1)^{1007}(1006,1006\sqrt3)=(-1006,-1006\sqrt3)$ for this choice, and reflecting in the $x$-axis gives $(-1006,1006\sqrt3)$.

**Answer: $(-1006,\,1006\sqrt3)$ and $(-1006,\,-1006\sqrt3)$**
